title: Beasts of Aethelgard – Truly Dangerous Creatures, Observation and Wonder
content:
The Truly Dangerous are those that actively hunt intelligent beings, not out of malice, but because intelligent beings are prey.

The manticores of the southern jungles of Kharakuna combine leonine bodies, bat-like wings, and scorpion tails. They have learned that caravans are easier to hunt than wild herds.

Chimeras are rare but devastating. They are said to be created when magic warps living creatures, fusing incompatible parts into forms that should not exist and cannot survive for long. But while they live, they kill with desperate fury those creatures that know they should not exist.

The undead, though not strictly beasts, inhabit places where the wounds of the Cataclysm run deep: skeletons rising from mass graves; ghosts clinging to ruins; Ghouls who were once human and now remember only hunger. They are not natural beings, and they are treated not as animals to be understood, but as cancers to be removed.

Observation and wonder remain the correct responses to most beasts of Aethelgard. The world is old, and life has had time to experiment.

A traveler might glimpse a unicorn in the deepest groves of the Sylvanweald. These are not the gentle creatures of children's tales, but wild creatures of pure magic; their horns wield power over life and death, and their temperament is as sharp as their beauty.

A sailor might spot a sea serpent surfacing far from shore; its scales catch the sunlight like scattered gems.

A miner can penetrate a cave inhabited by crystal snakes—their bodies are translucent, their movements silent, and their gaze devoid of threat, only the ancient, indifferent curiosity of creatures that have never learned to fear.

The beasts of Aethelgard are not monsters to be slain for experience or treasure (though both can be obtained from them). They are companions in the living world, shaped by the same Pulse that flows through elves, dwarves, and humans. They deserve the same respect that any intelligent race shows for forces they cannot fully control. A wise hunter takes only what he needs. A wise farmer builds fences strong enough to deter the curious, but not so strong as to completely block the way. A wise traveler observes, learns, and thanks fate that in a world of wonders, most wonders simply exist, demanding nothing from those who share them.
